reviewer.name: Claude Sonnet, fresh subagent (preservation reviewer)
reviewer.origin: Claude Agent tool subagent, model sonnet, a fresh context with only this brief and its files, launched 2026-10-26 by session_01Mxpoi6tFT3FgKmBvtGjRtS (the writer's session)

evidence: Compared DRAFT.txt with SOURCE.txt (his line 'Borrowed is fine, as long as it’s from someone steady who won’t try to run your trip for you', glossed as the Nurturer and Protector of the sentence before, borrowed from someone else) piece by piece, then read the draft in CONTEXT.txt, where it appears once, word for word, as the last sentence of the first paragraph, right after 'with enough Nurturer and Protector in the room before you go deep (see the inner child reparenting section).' His line has three parts and the draft keeps all three, in the same order and with the same actors: (1) borrowed support is allowed = 'Borrow some from someone else if you need to' (you borrow; the lender is someone other than you; 'some' picks up 'enough Nurturer and Protector' from the sentence before, so 'if you need to' restates that sentence’s own condition and does not add a new one); (2) the lender must be steady = 'make sure they’re stable' (near synonyms for a calm, dependable person; I do not read 'stable' as a stronger or weaker requirement here); (3) the lender must not try to run your trip for you = 'not someone who will try to direct your trip' (same negation, same actor; both mean the lender taking charge of your experience). Shifts I weighed: 'is fine' becomes a permissive imperative with 'if you need to', and 'as long as' becomes 'but make sure', so his condition becomes something the reader checks. I judged these ordinary paraphrase: the rule of conduct is the same (borrow if you lack support, only from someone steady who does not take over), no person, number, claim, reason or first-person fact comes in, and the only word of his with no counterpart is 'fine', whose job (that it is allowed) the permissive imperative does. The change is one sentence swapped for his one sentence with no fix, and the draft is that. Tell rows: went through T01-T29 and C01-C04 on the draft in its paragraph and found none actually happening. Weighed longest: T22 and T10 (the 'if you need to, but make sure' frame): not present, since the sentence carries his rule and a reason (a stable lender who does not take over), not reassurance alone, and 'if you need to' is anchored by the sentence before; T12 and T16 ('stable and not someone who will…'): his own two conditions of different kinds, not a matched pair or a reflex 'not X, it’s Y'; T02: the last of three sentences (a disclaimer, then two cautions) and, as in the source, not a run of compressed commands; T29 and T20: the sentence adds a new consideration (who to borrow from) and is neither a restatement nor a clever closer; T15: the swaps are to plain words. C02: 'some' is the Nurturer and Protector of the sentence before and 'they' is the someone else; on a fast read of an appendix about substances 'borrow some' could be misread as borrowing a substance, but 'sober first, with enough Nurturer and Protector in the room' sits right before it and his own 'Borrowed' leans on the same sentence, so I do not count it. Typography nit, not counted: a straight apostrophe in 'they’re' next to a curly 'I’d'; the article already mixes both (you've and it's time against it’s a protective part). Linter D9 (follows the source order): accepted, because one sentence swapped for one sentence with the same three points has to follow them in order, and the paragraph around it keeps his first-person reasoning and cross-reference. Linter E36/E41 (heavy second person, 8.3 per 100): accepted; it is two 'you' words ('if you need to', 'your trip') in 24 words in a safety caution, and his own line has the same two in 19 words (about 10.5 per 100), so the draft is lighter than the source; the whole appendix is addressed to 'you'.
